dialogs.title: Diálogo — ¿A qué hora te levantas?
dialogs.intro: Two people from two continents compare their mornings. It turns out the times are what differ most.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: What time do you get up?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Me levanto a las seis de la mañana.
lines.id: I get up at six in the morning.
lines.literal: I-raise-myself at the hours six of the morning.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Desayuno, me ducho y salgo a las siete.
lines.id: I have breakfast, shower and leave at seven.
lines.literal: I-breakfast, I-shower-myself and I-go-out at the hours seven.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: And how do you get to work?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voy en moto. Tardo media hora.
lines.id: I go by motorbike. It takes me half an hour.
lines.literal: I-go in motorbike. I-take half hour.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.id: Do you work in the morning?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Trabajo de ocho a cuatro. Después estudio español.
lines.id: I work from eight to four. Then I study Spanish.
lines.literal: I-work from eight to four. after I-study Spanish.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Nosotros cenamos muy tarde en España, a las diez.
lines.id: In Spain we have dinner very late, at ten.
lines.literal: we we-dine very late in Spain, at the hours ten.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: ¿A las diez? ¡A esa hora yo ya duermo!
lines.id: At ten? By then I'm already asleep!
lines.literal: at the hours ten? at that hour I already I-sleep!

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Entonces te acuestas a las nueve, ¿no?
lines.id: So you go to bed at nine, right?
lines.literal: then you-lay-yourself-down at the hours nine, no?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Casi siempre. Los viernes me acuesto más tarde.
lines.id: Almost always. On Fridays I go to bed later.
lines.literal: almost always. the Fridays I-lay-myself-down more late.

notes: **Clock times are plural.** *Son las tres* (it's three o'clock), *son las nueve* (it's nine) — because it means "the hours". The one exception is one o'clock, which is singular: *Es la una*.

**A qué hora vs qué hora.** *¿Qué hora es?* asks what time it is **now**; *¿A qué hora…?* asks what time something **happens**. The answers follow suit: *son las seis* for the first, *a las seis* for the second.

**De la mañana vs por la mañana.** Use *de* when a time is given (*a las seis de la mañana*, like "a.m."), and *por* when it isn't (*trabajo por la mañana* = I work in the morning). Getting it wrong isn't fatal, but it immediately sounds translated.

**Verbs that turn back on yourself.** *Levantar* = to raise, *levantarse* = to raise **yourself**, i.e. to get up. Only the little word in front changes: *me levanto, te levantas, se levanta*. The same goes for *ducharse* (to shower) and *llamarse* (to be called), which you've been using since Unit 2 without noticing.

**Some "I" forms misbehave.** *Salir* → *salgo*, *hacer* → *hago*, *poner* → *pongo*, *conocer* → *conozco*. Only the *yo* form is odd; the rest go back to normal (*sales, sale, salimos*). Learn them one by one as you meet them, not as a list.
**Tardar** = to take (time). *Tardo media hora* — it takes me half an hour. Very useful: Spanish turns English "it takes me" into one simple verb with *yo* as the subject.
**Los viernes** = "on Fridays, every Friday". A plural article in front of a day turns it into a habit. Without it, *el viernes* means this coming Friday.
**¿No? at the end of a sentence** works just like English "right?" — asking for agreement. Another option is *¿verdad?*

grammars.title: The six verb forms — now complete
body: In Unit 3 you used the first three forms, and in Unit 7 the *tener* table showed all six at once. Here's the full list, now with the pattern. Notice that the *nosotros* form always ends in **-mos** and the *ellos* form always in **-n** — two anchors that never change anywhere in Spanish:
after: *Vosotros* (informal "you all") only lives in Spain. All over Latin America people use *ustedes* for every group, informal or polite — so if you're heading to Mexico or Argentina, you can just recognize this row without mastering it.
One pattern that saves a lot of memorizing: the *nosotros* form of **-ar** and **-er** verbs uses the verb's own vowel (*trabajamos*, *comemos*), while **-ir** verbs use *-imos* (*vivimos*).

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs — me, te, se
body: Reflexive verbs (*verbos reflexivos*) describe actions that fall back on the person doing them. Their dictionary form always ends in **-se**: *levantarse*, *ducharse*, *acostarse*, *llamarse*. Not only the verb changes, but also the little word in front:
after: The little word goes **before** a conjugated verb: *me ducho*. But when the verb is still in its dictionary form, it attaches to the **end** as one word: *quiero ducharme*, *tengo que levantarme temprano*.
Some verbs change meaning when made reflexive: *ir* (to go) → *irse* (to leave), *dormir* (to sleep) → *dormirse* (to fall asleep), *llamar* (to call) → *llamarse* (to be called).

blocks.title: Ir — to go
items: *voy* (I go) · *vas* · *va* · *vamos* · *vais* · *van*. Completely irregular, and a must-learn because you'll use it every day.
*A + el* merges into *al*: *voy al trabajo*, *voy al cine*. With feminine places there's no merge: *voy a la oficina*.
Means of transport take *en* ("by"): *en moto*, *en coche*, *en autobús*, *en tren*, *en metro*. The one exception: *a pie* (on foot).
